🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Long ago, the Greeks told a story about a war. A Trojan prince named Paris carried off Helen, the wife of a Greek king, to his city of Troy. The Greeks sailed across the sea to bring her back, and they camped outside Troy's high walls for ten years.

The Iliad does not tell the whole war. It tells a few weeks near the end, and it is about one feeling: the anger of the greatest Greek fighter, Achilles. When the Greek leader Agamemnon insults him, Achilles refuses to fight. Without him the Greeks start to lose. Then Achilles' best friend, Patroclus, is killed by the Trojan hero Hector, and Achilles' anger turns into grief and revenge.

The poem is full of battles, and some of them are rough to read. The best parts for young readers are the quiet ones. Hector says goodbye to his wife and baby son on the city wall; the baby is frightened by the horsehair crest on his father's helmet, and Hector laughs and takes it off. At the very end, Hector's old father, King Priam, goes alone at night to Achilles' tent to ask for his son's body. Achilles thinks of his own father, and the two enemies weep together.

blocks.cap: Tap a book of the Iliad to see what happens in it. The line shows how Achilles' anger rises and changes.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Tell it like a bard. The Iliad was sung aloud for a long time before it was written down. Singers used repeated phrases to help them: "swift-footed Achilles", "Hector of the shining helmet", "rosy-fingered Dawn". Make up a repeated phrase for each person in your family ("Dad, maker of pancakes"), then tell the story of your morning using them. Did the phrases make it easier to keep going?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Nobody knows who Homer was. The Greeks believed he was a blind poet from Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey. Modern scholars agree on a few things: the Iliad grew out of a long tradition of oral poetry, sung by bards who learned the stories and the ways of telling them from older bards, and it reached something like its present form around 750 to 700 BC. It is in Greek hexameter verse, about 15,700 lines, later divided into 24 books.

The war it describes was set in the Bronze Age, centuries before Homer. Troy was a real city, at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey, excavated from 1870 on. It was destroyed more than once. How much of Homer's war happened is still argued over.

The first word of the poem in Greek is mēnin, "wrath" or "anger". That is the subject. Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks (Homer calls them Achaeans, Argives or Danaans), must give back a captive woman to her father, a priest of Apollo, to end a plague. To make up for it he takes Briseis, the captive given to Achilles. Achilles withdraws from the fighting and asks his mother, the sea goddess Thetis, to have Zeus let the Trojans win until the Greeks see what they have lost.

head: Books
What happens
rows: The armies, a duel between Paris and Menelaus, the Greek hero Diomedes' great day, Hector's farewell to Andromache.
The Trojans drive the Greeks back to their ships. An embassy (Book 9) begs Achilles to return; he refuses.
Patroclus fights in Achilles' armor and is killed by Hector.
Achilles returns, with new armor made by the god Hephaestus, and kills Hector.
Funeral games for Patroclus; Priam ransoms Hector's body; Hector's funeral.

blocks.html: Homer gives the Trojans as much honor as the Greeks. Hector is fighting for his city, his wife and his son. In Book 6 he prays for the baby Astyanax:

The hero's choice. Achilles knows he has two possible fates: a short life with glory that lasts forever, or a long, quiet life that is forgotten. Glory (kleos) and honor (timē) drive the whole quarrel: Agamemnon's insult was an attack on Achilles' honor.
The poem does not end with the fall of Troy. It ends with two enemies. Priam, guided by the god Hermes, comes to Achilles' hut and kneels:
Achilles gives back the body and grants a truce for the funeral. His anger, which began the poem, ends in pity. The last line is about Hector's burial.

The Greeks learned to read on Homer. For a thousand years the Iliad was the shared book of the Greek world, quoted by philosophers, historians and generals. Plato, later on this ladder, both loved Homer and argued that his stories of quarreling gods were bad for the young.
Thinking the Iliad tells the Trojan horse story. It doesn't: the horse comes up briefly in the Odyssey and is told in full by Virgil in the Aeneid. The Iliad also ends before Achilles' death.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Was there one Homer, or many? In 1795 the German scholar F. A. Wolf argued that the poems were stitched together from shorter songs. In the 1920s and 1930s the American scholar Milman Parry showed how the repeated epithets ("swift-footed Achilles") fit the meter like building blocks, the tools of a singer composing as he performs. With Albert Lord he recorded oral poets in Yugoslavia who could sing long epics this way. Most scholars now think the Iliad comes from that kind of tradition, shaped by one or more great poets, and fixed in writing at some point; when and how are still debated.

The Iliad is a war poem that never pretends war is simple. It gives the names and homes of the men who die, often with a line about the parents who will never see them again. Its long similes compare battle to storms, harvests and fires, reminding the listener of the peaceful world outside. The Shield of Achilles in Book 18 shows a city at peace with a wedding and a court case beside a city at war.

items: Is Achilles right to refuse to fight after he is insulted? When does pride become a fault?
Why does the poem end with Priam and Achilles instead of the fall of Troy?
Can a poem honor both sides of a war?
The gods take sides and quarrel. Does that make the human choices matter less, or more?

blocks.html: Later books answer back. Virgil's Aeneid retells the war from the Trojan side. Plato's Republic questions what Homer teaches. Aristotle's Poetics praises Homer for giving the Iliad one unified action. Simone Weil's essay "The Iliad, or the Poem of Force" (1940) read it as a poem about what violence does to everyone it touches.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Achilles stops fighting because his honor was hurt. Have you ever refused to help because you felt treated unfairly? How did it turn out?
  2. Hector fights for his family and city even though he fears he will lose. Is that brave, or something else?
  3. Why do you think Achilles gives Hector's body back to Priam?
  4. Homer makes the enemy side human and sympathetic. Why might that be hard for people at war, and why might it matter?
  5. The Iliad was sung and memorized for generations before it was written down. What stories in your family are passed on by telling, not by writing?

The voyages of Books 9–12 and the homecoming scenes with Telemachus, Argos and Penelope suit young readers best.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

After the Trojan War, the Greek heroes sailed home. One of them, clever Odysseus, king of the small rocky island of Ithaca, took ten more years to get there. The Odyssey is the story of that trip, and of his wife Penelope and son Telemachus, who waited for him.

On the way, Odysseus meets wonders and monsters: a one-eyed giant called a Cyclops, a witch named Circe who turns his men into pigs, singing Sirens whose song lures sailors onto the rocks, and a six-headed monster and a whirlpool on either side of a narrow strait. He gets out of trouble mostly by thinking. He tells the Cyclops his name is "Nobody", so that when the giant shouts for help, he cries, "Nobody is hurting me!" and no one comes.

blocks.cap: Follow Odysseus' voyage stop by stop. Most of the places are legends; the map shows where ancient and modern readers have guessed they were.

blocks.html: At home, a crowd of rude young men are eating up his food and pestering Penelope to marry one of them. She tricks them for years: she says she will choose after she finishes weaving a burial cloth for Odysseus' father, and every night she secretly unpicks what she wove that day. When Odysseus finally comes home in disguise as an old beggar, the first to know him is his old dog, Argos.

🧩 Try this

Draw your own odyssey. Draw a map of a trip you have taken, even to the park or a grandparent's house. Mark the stops, and give each one an adventure (real or made up). Then tell the story to someone, starting in the middle, the way Homer does, and go back to explain how you got there.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

The Odyssey, like the Iliad, comes from the oral poetry of early Greece and is credited to Homer; it probably took its present shape a little after the Iliad, around 725 BC. It has 24 books and about 12,100 lines of hexameter verse. Where the Iliad is about a few weeks of war, the Odyssey is about getting home, and about who a person is when no one recognizes him.

Odysseus' usual epithet is polytropos, "of many turns", which Butler renders as "ingenious". He is the hero of cunning, disguise and patience. It was his idea, in later tellings, to build the wooden horse that ended the war.

The poem does not start at the beginning. Books 1–4 follow Telemachus, now grown, as he travels to find news of his father. Book 5 finds Odysseus himself, kept for seven years on the island of the nymph Calypso. Freed at last, he is shipwrecked on the island of the Phaeacians, and in Books 9–12 he tells his hosts the story of his wanderings. Books 13–24 bring him home to Ithaca.

blocks.html: At the Cyclops' cave, Odysseus is trapped with his men by the giant Polyphemus, a son of the sea god Poseidon. When the giant asks his name:

The trick saves them, but as he sails away Odysseus cannot resist shouting his real name. Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon, and the god's anger is the reason Odysseus' journey takes so long. Cleverness wins; pride costs.

Athena, the goddess who loves Odysseus for his intelligence, disguises him as an old beggar. He tests who has stayed loyal: the swineherd Eumaeus, his son, his old nurse Eurycleia (who knows him by a scar), and his dog.

Penelope sets a contest: whoever can string Odysseus' great bow and shoot through twelve axe heads may marry her. Only the beggar can. Odysseus then fights the suitors, with Telemachus beside him, and wins back his house. Penelope still tests him herself: she asks for their bed to be moved, and he angrily says it cannot be, because he built it around the trunk of a living olive tree. Only the two of them knew that.

Guest-friendship (xenia). The Greeks held that strangers and guests must be welcomed, fed and helped, and that Zeus protects them. Much of the Odyssey tests this rule: the Phaeacians and Eumaeus keep it; the Cyclops and the suitors break it.
Thinking Odysseus spends all twenty years at sea. Ten years were the war at Troy. Of the ten years coming home, seven were spent on Calypso's island.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Ithaca is a real island in the Ionian Sea, but Homer's descriptions of it don't fit it perfectly, and people have argued since ancient times about the geography of the poem. Ancient writers already placed the Cyclops in Sicily and Scylla and Charybdis at the Strait of Messina. The geographer Eratosthenes (3rd century BC) joked that you would find the scene of Odysseus' wanderings when you found the cobbler who stitched the bag of winds. The map in this lesson shows traditional guesses, not facts.

Some scenes are grim: the Cyclops eats several of Odysseus' men, and the end of the poem includes a harsh punishment of the suitors and of servants who sided with them. Readers have long debated whether Odysseus' revenge goes too far. The poem itself ends with Athena stopping a new cycle of fighting and making peace.

items: Is Odysseus a hero, a trickster, or both? Is lying ever the right thing to do?
Penelope is as clever as her husband. Who is the real hero of the poem?
What makes a place home? Why does Odysseus turn down Calypso's offer to make him immortal?
What do we owe strangers who come to our door?

blocks.html: Later writers kept sailing with Odysseus. Virgil's Aeneas visits some of the same places. In Dante's Inferno, later on this ladder, Ulysses tells of a last voyage beyond the known world. Tennyson's poem "Ulysses" (1842) has the old king ready to set out again.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Odysseus gets out of the Cyclops' cave by a trick, then nearly ruins it by boasting. When has showing off cost you something?
  2. Penelope waits twenty years and keeps her suitors guessing. What qualities does she need for that?
  3. The dog Argos knows Odysseus when no one else does. Why do you think Homer put that scene in?
  4. Which adventure would you most like to have had, and which would you most like to have avoided?
  5. How should guests behave, and how should hosts? Which characters in the Odyssey get it right?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In ancient Athens, plays were part of a great spring festival for the god Dionysus. Thousands of people sat on a hillside to watch, and poets competed for a prize. Aeschylus was the first great writer of tragedies, serious plays about gods, kings and hard choices.

His most famous work is three plays told together, the Oresteia. It is the story of a royal family with a curse on it. When King Agamemnon comes home from the Trojan War, his wife Clytemnestra kills him, because years before he sacrificed their daughter to get winds for his ships. Their son Orestes grows up and takes revenge on his mother. Then the Furies, spirits of revenge, hunt Orestes. It looks as if the killing will never stop.

Then something new happens. The goddess Athena says: let's have a trial. She picks citizens of Athens to be a jury, hears both sides, and the vote decides. Even the angry Furies are persuaded to accept it, and they become protectors of the city. Revenge gives way to a court of law.

blocks.cap: The family of Atreus. Tap a name to learn who they are; choose a play to see who is in it.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Hold a trial. Pick a small family argument (who gets the last cookie, whose turn it is to choose the movie). One person speaks for each side, and everyone else is the jury and votes. Afterward, talk about it: was a vote fairer than letting the loudest person win? What made a good argument?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BC) was born at Eleusis, near Athens. He fought against the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC, where his brother was killed, and probably at Salamis in 480 BC. He wrote perhaps 70 to 90 plays and won first prize at the festival of Dionysus about 13 times. Only seven of his plays survive, and one of those, Prometheus Bound, may not be his. Aristotle says he added a second actor, which made real dialogue possible. He died at Gela in Sicily; his epitaph, as reported later, recalls his courage at Marathon and says nothing of his plays.

The Oresteia (458 BC) is the only complete trilogy of Greek tragedy that survives: Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers (Choephori) and The Eumenides. It won first prize. A fourth, comic "satyr play" performed with it is lost.
A watchman on the palace roof at Argos waits, night after night, for a chain of beacon fires to signal that Troy has fallen:
The chorus of old men remembers how Agamemnon, ten years before, sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia when the goddess Artemis held back the winds his fleet needed. They search for meaning in suffering:

Agamemnon returns with the Trojan princess Cassandra, a prophet no one believes. Clytemnestra welcomes him with a purple carpet and kills him offstage, with her ally Aegisthus, Agamemnon's cousin and an heir of the family feud. The audience hears it rather than sees it.

blocks.text: The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides

blocks.html: Years later Orestes returns in secret and meets his sister Electra at their father's tomb. Commanded by Apollo, he kills Aegisthus and his mother. At once the Furies (Erinyes), ancient goddesses who punish crimes against kin, begin to hunt him.
In the third play Orestes flees to Apollo's shrine at Delphi and then to Athens. Athena does not judge the case herself. She founds a court on the Areopagus, the Hill of Ares, with citizen jurors:

The votes are equal; Athena's deciding vote frees Orestes. The Furies threaten the land, but Athena persuades them with offers of honor, and they accept a home in Athens as the Eumenides, "the Kindly Ones".

From vengeance to justice. In the first two plays, each killing answers the last, and each killer believes justice is on his or her side. The trilogy ends when the cycle passes to a public court: evidence, argument, a vote, and an outcome both sides must accept.

Athenians watching in 458 BC knew the real Areopagus council, whose powers had just been cut back in reforms of 462/1 BC. Scholars still debate whether the play supports, regrets or simply accepts those reforms.
Thinking the Furies are simply defeated. They are not driven out; they are given an honored place. The play suggests that a city still needs some respect and fear of wrongdoing, under the law.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Three poets were chosen each year for the City Dionysia. Each presented three tragedies and a satyr play on one day. The actors were all men, wore masks, and could play several parts each. The chorus, twelve in Aeschylus' day, sang and danced between the scenes. Violent acts happened offstage and were reported or revealed afterward.

items: Clytemnestra, Orestes and the Furies all claim to be doing justice. Can more than one side be right?
Why does Athena found a court instead of deciding the case herself?
Is "wisdom comes by suffering" a comfort or a warning?
What is the difference between revenge and punishment?

blocks.html: Sophocles and Euripides both wrote their own Electra, each telling the same revenge differently, which you can compare on the next rungs. Aristotle's Poetics studies how tragedies like these work. In the Middle Ages and after, the idea that a court, not a family, should answer a killing became a basic principle of law.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. In the trilogy, each act of revenge leads to another. How do people stop a cycle like that, in families or between countries?
  2. Athena asks ordinary citizens to be the jury. Why might that be better than letting a god or a king decide?
  3. The jury's vote is a tie. Is it fair that Athena's vote decides?
  4. The Furies are offered honor instead of being punished. Why might that work better?
  5. The watchman waits a whole year for a signal fire. What is the longest you have waited for news?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Oedipus the King turns on a terrible discovery: without knowing it, Oedipus killed his father and married his mother. Jocasta's death and Oedipus' blinding happen offstage. Summarize these simply for young readers; Antigone's choice and the riddle of the Sphinx are the best starting points.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Sophocles lived in Athens when it was at its height, and wrote more than a hundred plays. Seven survive. Two of the most famous are about one unlucky royal family of the city of Thebes.

In Oedipus the King, a terrible sickness has struck Thebes. King Oedipus, who once saved the city by answering the riddle of a monster called the Sphinx, promises to find out what caused it. A message from the god Apollo says: find the man who killed the old king. Oedipus is a great puzzle-solver, and he will not stop asking questions, even when people beg him to. The answer turns out to be the worst possible: he himself, without knowing it, is the man he is hunting.

In Antigone, Oedipus' daughter Antigone faces a hard choice. Her two brothers have killed each other in a war over the throne. The new king, Creon, says one brother may be buried but the other, who attacked the city, must be left unburied. Antigone believes the gods require every family to bury its dead, so she buries him anyway, and she will not say she is sorry. Is she right to break the king's law?

🧩 Try this

Solve the riddle. The old story says the Sphinx asked: What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening? Oedipus answered: a human being, who crawls as a baby, walks upright as a grown-up, and uses a cane when old. Make up a riddle of your own about something in your house, and try it on your family.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Sophocles (c. 496–406 BC) was from Colonus, just outside Athens. His long life spanned the city's golden age: he was a teenager at the time of Salamis and died two years before Athens lost the Peloponnesian War. He was elected one of the city's generals, serving with Pericles around 441 BC, and won first prize at the festival of Dionysus around 20 times, more than any other tragedian. Ancient sources say he wrote about 123 plays. Aristotle credits him with adding a third actor.

Seven plays survive: Ajax, Antigone (c. 441 BC), The Women of Trachis, Oedipus the King (also called Oedipus Tyrannus, c. 429 BC), Electra, Philoctetes (409 BC) and Oedipus at Colonus (staged after his death, in 401 BC). The three Theban plays are often read together, but they were written many years apart and are not a trilogy.

The play is built like a detective story in which the detective is also the culprit. Step by step, the prophet Tiresias, Queen Jocasta, a messenger from Corinth and an old shepherd each supply a piece. Oedipus learns that he was the baby abandoned long ago because of a prophecy, that the stranger he killed in a quarrel on the road was his father, King Laius, and that the queen he married is his mother. Jocasta dies, and Oedipus blinds himself. The chorus ends the play:

Reversal and recognition. Aristotle's Poetics holds up Oedipus as the model tragedy: the messenger who comes to cheer Oedipus brings the opposite (a reversal, peripeteia), at the very moment Oedipus learns the truth (a recognition, anagnorisis).
Antigone tells Creon why she disobeyed him:

Creon sentences her to be shut in a rock tomb. His son Haemon, who is engaged to Antigone, pleads with him; the prophet Tiresias warns him. Creon gives way too late: Antigone, Haemon and Creon's wife all die, and Creon is left alone. Earlier, the chorus sings a famous ode on human cleverness, which can master sea and land but not death:

Antigone has been read as the first great drama about conscience against the state: a law made by a ruler set against a law the person believes is higher. It is also a play about stubbornness on both sides, which is why readers still disagree about it.

Reading Oedipus as a man who was simply punished for a sin. The play never says the gods made him a bad man. He acts in ignorance, and his great strengths, his intelligence and his refusal to stop asking, are what bring the truth out.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Was Oedipus free? The prophecy came true, but every step he took toward it he chose: to leave Corinth, to fight on the road, to accept the throne, to keep investigating. Ancient and modern readers have argued over how fate and choice fit together in the play. It does not settle the question; it makes the audience feel it.

The philosopher G. W. F. Hegel, in the early 1800s, read Antigone as a clash between two real goods, duty to family and the gods on one side and the order of the city on the other, each pushed too far. Others see Antigone as plainly right and Creon as plainly wrong. Both readings have long histories.

items: Is it ever right to break a law? How would you decide?
Antigone cites "unwritten laws". Are there laws no ruler can change?
Oedipus would not stop searching for the truth. Is it always better to know?
Why might the chorus say no one should be called happy until the end of their life?

blocks.html: Herodotus, on a later rung, tells the same idea through the wise Athenian Solon and the rich king Croesus. Aristotle's Poetics and Plato's dialogues return again and again to these plays. The idea of an unwritten higher law runs on to Cicero, Aquinas and the natural-law thinkers later on this ladder.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Oedipus keeps asking questions even when others beg him to stop. When is it good to keep digging for the truth, and when is it not?
  2. Antigone breaks the king's law to do what she thinks is right. Was she right? What would you have done?
  3. Creon changes his mind, but too late. What makes it hard for people in charge to admit they were wrong?
  4. "Wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man." What human inventions do you find most wonderful?
  5. Why do people still enjoy plays and stories that end sadly?

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Euripides was the youngest of the three great writers of Greek tragedy. He liked to show the old stories from a new angle: from the side of the people who lost, the women left behind, the servants, the enemies. His audiences didn't always like it, and he won the big prize only a few times. But after he died, his plays became the most popular of all.

Some of his plays have happy endings. In Alcestis, a queen agrees to die in her husband's place, and the strong hero Heracles wrestles Death himself to bring her back. In Helen, it turns out that the real Helen never went to Troy at all: the gods sent a look-alike made of cloud, while the real Helen waited in Egypt, and her husband finds her there after the war. In Iphigenia among the Taurians, a sister and brother who think each other lost meet in a faraway land and escape together.

Other plays are very sad. The Trojan Women shows the queens and princesses of Troy on the day after the city falls, waiting to learn which Greek they will be given to as captives. It asks the audience to feel the pain of the losing side.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Tell it from the other side. Pick a fairy tale you know, like "The Three Little Pigs" or "Jack and the Beanstalk". Retell it from the point of view of the wolf or the giant. Does the story change? Euripides did this with the old Greek myths.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Euripides (c. 480–406 BC) was an Athenian. A later legend says he was born on the island of Salamis on the very day of the battle there, in 480 BC. He wrote about 90 plays; 18 tragedies (one of them, Rhesus, perhaps by someone else) and one satyr play, The Cyclops, survive under his name, more than for Aeschylus and Sophocles together, partly because some of his plays were chosen for reading in schools and partly by luck. He won first prize only four times in his life. Near the end he left Athens for the court of King Archelaus of Macedon, where he died.

Date
In brief
rows: A wife gives her life for her husband; Heracles brings her back.
Abandoned by Jason, a foreign princess takes a terrible revenge.
A young man's vow and a stepmother's secret love destroy a family.
The women of Troy the day after its fall.
The real Helen in Egypt; a phantom went to Troy.
The god Dionysus comes to Thebes and punishes a king who rejects him.

blocks.html: Medea opens with the heroine's old nurse wishing the whole story had never begun, with Jason's famous quest for the Golden Fleece:

Medea, a princess of Colchis on the Black Sea, had helped Jason win the Fleece and fled with him to Greece. Now he leaves her to marry the daughter of the king of Corinth, and she is to be exiled. She takes revenge on everyone Jason loves, including, in the play's most shocking turn, their own children, and escapes in the chariot of her grandfather the Sun. The play makes Medea frightening and also lets her speak powerfully about how women, wives and foreigners were treated.

In 415 BC, the year after Athens captured the island of Melos (on the Thucydides rung), Euripides staged a play about the victims of a captured city. Hecuba, the old queen of Troy, holds the body of her little grandson, killed by the Greeks because they fear he might grow up to rebuild Troy:
Whether the play was a protest against Melos is debated; it was probably written before or soon after. What is clear is that it asked an Athenian audience, at war, to feel for the defeated.

Gods from the machine. Euripides often ends a play with a god appearing above the stage on a crane (the mēchanē) to settle things. Later critics used the Latin phrase deus ex machina, "a god from the machine", for any too-convenient ending.

Thinking Euripides was against the gods or against women. Ancient comedians said so, and so have some modern readers. His plays let characters argue every side, often brilliantly, and leave the verdict to the audience.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Aristotle's Poetics calls Euripides "the most tragic of the poets", even while criticizing how he built his plots. It also reports that Sophocles said he showed people as they ought to be, and Euripides as they are. Aristophanes, on the next rung, mocked him in The Frogs and other comedies as a clever talker who brought ordinary people and household matters onto the tragic stage.

Plutarch's life of the Athenian general Nicias tells that after the Athenian disaster in Sicily in 413 BC, some captured Athenians won food or even freedom by reciting Euripides, whose verses the Sicilian Greeks loved. Whether or not it is true, it shows how far his fame spread.

Medea and The Bacchae end in killings within a family, and Hippolytus turns on an unwanted love. As in all Greek tragedy, the violence happens offstage. For families, Alcestis, Helen and Iphigenia among the Taurians are good first plays.

items: Does seeing a story from the losers' side change who you think is right?
Can a character be both a victim and a villain?
Is an ending in which a god fixes everything satisfying, or a cheat?
Why might a playwright's work become more popular after his death?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Euripides tells old stories from the side of the people who lost. Can you think of a book or film that does that?
  2. In The Trojan Women, the Greeks fear that a child might grow up to take revenge. Is fear a good reason to do something?
  3. Medea was a foreigner in Greece. How do the other characters treat her because of it?
  4. Which ending do you prefer: one where the characters fix things themselves, or one where a god steps in?
  5. Why do you think the Sicilians might have spared prisoners who could recite poetry?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Ancient comedy has a lot of crude humor. This lesson quotes and summarizes only family-suitable parts. The Birds (the sky city) and The Frogs (the frog chorus and the contest of poets) have the best scenes for families, read in selections.

Choose a path

  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In Athens, the same festivals that showed tragedies also showed comedies, and the funniest writer of them was Aristophanes. His plays are wild fantasies: two Athenians fed up with their city persuade the birds to build a city in the clouds; a farmer flies to heaven on a giant dung beetle to bring back the goddess Peace; the god Dionysus goes down to the land of the dead to fetch back a good poet, because there are none left in Athens.

He made fun of everyone: the city's leaders, its generals, its poets, its teachers, and the audience itself. The actors wore padded costumes and masks, and the chorus dressed up as birds, wasps, clouds or frogs.

blocks.name: gb-old-comedy
blocks.cap: The parts of an Old Comedy, using The Birds as the example. Tap each part.

blocks.html: Some of his jokes are rude, the way a lot of slapstick is, so grown-ups usually choose the scenes. The Birds and The Frogs have the best family scenes: the birds building their sky city, and the chorus of frogs who croak "Brekekekex, ko-ax, ko-ax!" at Dionysus as he rows across the lake of the dead.

🧩 Try this

Write a sky city. In The Birds, the new city in the clouds is called Cloudcuckooland. Invent your own city in an impossible place (under the sea, on the Moon, inside a teapot). What is it called? Who lives there? What are its three silliest laws? Act out a visitor arriving.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Aristophanes (c. 446–c. 386 BC) wrote about 40 comedies; eleven survive, the only complete examples of the "Old Comedy" of Athens. Most were written during the Peloponnesian War, and the war, peace and the city's leaders are never far away. In The Acharnians (425 BC) a farmer makes his own private peace with Sparta. In The Knights (424 BC) he attacked the powerful politician Cleon, who, Aristophanes says, had taken him to court over an earlier play.

Date
The fantasy
rows: A father sends his son to Socrates' "Thinkery" to learn to win any argument.
An old man is addicted to serving on juries.
A farmer flies a giant beetle to heaven to rescue the goddess Peace.
Two Athenians found Cloudcuckooland and cut the gods off from mankind.
Dionysus goes to the underworld to bring back a poet.
The blind god of wealth is cured, and riches go to the honest.

blocks.html: Sophocles and Euripides had both died in 406 BC. In The Frogs, the god of the theater, Dionysus, decides Athens needs a great poet and sets off for the underworld with his slave Xanthias, who opens the play by asking which tired old jokes he may use:
Rowing across the lake of the dead, Dionysus is mocked by a chorus of frogs:

In the underworld he finds Aeschylus and Euripides quarreling over the chair of best tragedian. A contest follows: the two poets quote, criticize and parody each other's verses, and finally weigh lines on a giant scale. Dionysus chooses Aeschylus, the poet of the generation that beat the Persians, to bring back to Athens. The play won first prize, and ancient sources say it was given the rare honor of a second performance because of the serious advice its chorus gave the city.

The parabasis. In the middle of an Old Comedy the actors leave and the chorus steps forward to speak straight to the audience, often for the poet himself: praise of his own plays, complaints about rivals, and advice to the city. It is a little like a comedian dropping the act.

The Clouds shows Socrates hanging in a basket to study the sky and teaching young men to make the weaker argument defeat the stronger. The real Socrates did none of this, and he later complained, in Plato's Apology (later on this ladder), that the play had helped give people a false picture of him. Plato's Symposium nonetheless shows Aristophanes and Socrates at the same dinner party, on friendly terms.
Aristophanes is our best window into everyday Athens: its law courts, markets, assembly, festivals, prices and slang. Historians use his jokes as evidence, carefully, since a joke exaggerates.
Taking the comedies as a fair report. Aristophanes was a satirist. His Socrates, his Euripides and his Cleon are cartoons, drawn for laughs, and readers have to check them against other sources.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

All eleven comedies have crude humor, and some (for example Lysistrata, about women who go on strike to end the war) build whole plots on it. Parents may want to read selections: the frog chorus, the contest of the poets in The Frogs, the founding of Cloudcuckooland in The Birds, and the rescue of Peace.

Old Comedy could name and mock living, powerful people in front of thousands of citizens. Ancient writers already disagreed about how free it was: some reported attempts to limit mockery by name, and Aristophanes says he was prosecuted by Cleon. After Athens lost the war, comedy turned toward plots about ordinary families; the "New Comedy" of Menander, a century later, is the ancestor of the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence and, through them, of modern situation comedy.

items: Can a joke be unfair? Is it different when the target is powerful?
Why might laughing at a city's leaders be good for the city? Can it also do harm?
In The Frogs, a comedy argues about what makes a great tragedy. Can comedy be serious?
Was it fair of Aristophanes to put a real person, Socrates, on stage as a fraud?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Aristophanes invented a city in the clouds. If you could found a new city, what would its laws be?
  2. Why do people enjoy jokes about famous or powerful people? Where is the line between fun and unkind?
  3. The frogs keep croaking to annoy Dionysus. What is the most annoying sound you know, and how would you put it in a play?
  4. Socrates said the comedy gave people the wrong idea about him. Can a funny story spread a false picture? Can you think of an example?
  5. In The Frogs, Dionysus chooses the older poet. Do you think old books or new books have more to teach?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The Histories describe battles and some cruel customs and punishments, in a matter-of-fact way. This lesson keeps to the main story. Young readers enjoy Book II (Egypt) and the tales in Book I, read aloud with a parent choosing the passages.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

About 2,500 years ago, a man named Herodotus set out to answer a big question: why did the Greeks and the Persians go to war? To find out, he traveled and asked questions everywhere he went, in Egypt, around the Black Sea, in the cities of Greece and Asia Minor. Then he wrote it all down. His book is the oldest great history we have, and the Greek word he used for it, historiē, meant "inquiry", finding out by asking. That is where our word history comes from.

The Persian Empire was the biggest the world had seen. Its kings, Darius and then his son Xerxes, sent huge armies against the Greeks, who lived in many small, quarrelsome cities. Against the odds, the Greeks won: at Marathon in 490 BC, and ten years later in the sea battle of Salamis. Before Salamis, a small band of Spartans and their allies held the narrow pass of Thermopylae for three days.

blocks.cap: Herodotus' world. Step through the wars, or tap a place.

blocks.html: Herodotus loved a good story, and he put them all in: a clever thief who outwits the king of Egypt, a musician rescued by a dolphin, ants as big as foxes that dig for gold. Sometimes he says plainly that he doesn't believe a story he was told, but he writes it down anyway, so his readers can judge.

🧩 Try this

Be a historian. Choose an event from before you were born: how your grandparents met, the day your town got its library, a family move. Ask two or three people who remember it. Do their stories match? Write down what they agree on, and where they differ. That is what Herodotus did.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Herodotus (c. 484–c. 425 BC) was born in Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum, in Turkey), a Greek city then under Persian rule. He traveled widely and later joined the new Athenian-led colony of Thurii in southern Italy. The Roman writer Cicero called him "the father of history". His work, written in the Ionic dialect of Greek, was later divided into nine books, each named for one of the nine Muses.
He set out to do two things at once: to keep great deeds from being forgotten, and to explain causes. That second aim is what makes him a historian and not only a storyteller.

Subject
rows: Croesus of Lydia; the rise of Cyrus the Great and Persia.
Egypt: the Nile, the pyramids, customs and kings.
Cambyses and Darius; the Scythians of the steppes, and Libya.
The Ionian Greeks revolt (499 BC); Darius' expedition and Marathon (490 BC).
Xerxes' invasion: Thermopylae and Artemisium, Salamis (480 BC), Plataea and Mycale (479 BC).

blocks.cap: The invasions of 490 and 480 BC. Step through the campaign; each step notes the book of the Histories that tells it.

blocks.html: Book I tells how Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia, asked the Athenian lawgiver Solon who was the happiest man in the world, expecting to hear his own name. Solon named ordinary people who had lived and died well, and warned:
Croesus later lost his kingdom to Cyrus of Persia. (The dates suggest the two men could hardly have met; Herodotus tells the story for its lesson.) Sophocles' Oedipus ends with the same thought.

In 480 BC Xerxes led his army into Greece. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, King Leonidas of Sparta, with his 300 Spartans and several thousand allies, held them for three days, until a local man named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass. Leonidas sent most of the allies away and stayed to fight. Herodotus records a Spartan's answer to the news that Persian arrows would hide the sun:

Freedom and law. For Herodotus, the war was a contest between a great empire ruled by one man and small cities governed by their own laws. In one scene the exiled Spartan king Demaratus tells Xerxes that the Spartans are free, but not wholly free, because they fear their law more than Xerxes' subjects fear him.

Herodotus treats the Persians, Egyptians and Scythians with real curiosity. He says that if all people were asked to choose the best customs, each would choose their own, and he takes that as a reason for respect, not contempt.

Thinking Herodotus believed every story he told. He often says "the Persians say", "the Egyptians say", or "this I do not believe", and he sometimes gives two or three versions. He reports; the reader is meant to weigh.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Thucydides, on the next rung, seems to have Herodotus in mind when he complains about history written to please listeners. Plutarch, centuries later, wrote a whole essay, "On the Malice of Herodotus", accusing him of bias. Modern archaeology has confirmed much of what he reports, for example about Egypt and the Scythians, and shown other parts to be wrong or legendary. Historians today treat him as an invaluable source who must be read with care, which is what he asked for.

items: Is a history better if it leaves out the stories it can't prove, or if it includes them with a warning?
Herodotus says each people thinks its own customs best. Is that a reason to respect other customs, or to doubt all of them?
Why might small cities have beaten a vast empire?
Can we ever know the true cause of a war?

blocks.html: Thucydides set a stricter standard; Plutarch's Lives retell many of the same people, Themistocles, Aristides and others, on the Rome rungs. Herodotus' account of Egypt is still read on the site's Egyptology Ladder.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Herodotus asked many people the same question and wrote down all their answers. Why is it useful to hear more than one side?
  2. Which of Herodotus' stories would you most like to be true?
  3. The Spartans at Thermopylae stayed when they could have left. What do you think of their choice?
  4. Solon says no one should be called happy until the end of life. Do you agree?
  5. If someone wrote the history of your family, what would you want them to be sure to get right?

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Fifty years after the Greeks beat the Persians, the two strongest Greek cities went to war with each other: Athens, a democracy with a great navy and an empire of island allies, and Sparta, a city of soldiers with the best army in Greece and its own league of allies. The war lasted 27 years, from 431 to 404 BC, and Sparta won.

An Athenian named Thucydides wrote its history. He was there: he caught the terrible plague that struck Athens, and he commanded ships in the war. When he failed to save a city from the Spartans, the Athenians sent him away, and he spent twenty years in exile, which gave him time to talk to people on both sides.

Thucydides wanted to get things exactly right. He didn't put in stories about gods or monsters. He checked what people told him, because, he said, eyewitnesses often remember the same event differently. He hoped his book would be useful long after his own time, to anyone who wanted to understand how wars start and what they do to people.

blocks.cap: Athens and its allies against Sparta and its allies. Step through the war, or tap a city.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Two eyewitnesses. Have two people watch the same short scene (a pet, the street outside, a minute of a ball game), then each write down, without talking, exactly what happened. Compare. What did both notice? What did only one see? Thucydides said that is why a historian must check every account.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: A history written from inside the war

blocks.html: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC) was a wealthy Athenian with family ties to Thrace. He survived the plague of 430 BC and was elected a general in 424 BC; when the Spartan commander Brasidas took the city of Amphipolis before he could arrive, he was exiled for twenty years. His history, later divided into eight books, breaks off in 411 BC, seven years before the war ended. The historian Xenophon carried the story on.

Method. In Book I, Thucydides explains that he checked reports of events as carefully as he could, because witnesses disagree and memory is partial. For speeches, he says, he gives what each speaker most likely said, keeping as close as he could to the general sense. He hopes his work will be "a possession for all time", useful because human nature makes such things happen again.
He also separates the stated quarrels that set off the war from what he calls its truest cause: the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

blocks.html: At the public funeral after the first year of war, the Athenian leader Pericles praised not the dead men one by one but the city they died for: a democracy, he said, where power rests with the many, where people are judged by merit, where citizens take part in public affairs and the city is open to the world, "the school of Hellas". It is one of the most famous speeches in history, and also, as Thucydides shows by what comes next, an ideal: the plague strikes Athens the very next summer.
In 416 BC Athens demanded that the small neutral island of Melos join its empire. Thucydides writes the negotiation as a dialogue. The Melians appeal to justice and the gods. The Athenians answer:

Melos refused, was besieged and fell; the Athenians put the men to death and enslaved the women and children. In the next book, Athens sets out with great confidence to conquer Sicily, and loses its fleet and army.

Thucydides does not tell the reader what to think. He sets speeches side by side (Pericles and the Spartan king Archidamus; Cleon and Diodotus on Mytilene; the Athenians and the Melians) and lets events answer them. Readers have argued ever since about what his own view was.
Treating the speeches as word-for-word records. Thucydides says plainly that they are his reconstructions of what was said, or of what the occasion called for.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Describing civil strife at Corcyra in 427 BC, Thucydides says that war is a violent teacher: in hard times, people's tempers sink to their circumstances, and even the meanings of words change, so that reckless daring is called loyal courage and caution is called cowardice. He gives the plague the same cool attention, describing its symptoms so that it could be recognized if it ever came again.

The book describes the plague, massacres and the fate of the defeated, plainly and without sensation. Parents may want to preview Books II (the plague), III (Corcyra), V (Melos) and VII (the end in Sicily). For young readers, the Funeral Oration and the story of the Sicilian Expedition read aloud work well.

items: Is it true that the strong do what they can? Should it be? Who in the history seems to think otherwise?
What is the difference between a stated reason for a war and its real cause?
Can a democracy run an empire and stay a democracy?
Is history useful for the future, as Thucydides hoped, or does every age face new problems?

blocks.html: Thomas Hobbes, later on this ladder, made the first English translation directly from the Greek (1629) and said Thucydides taught him how dangerous democracy could be. Others have read him as the great defender of Athenian freedom. Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Politics, on the next rungs, take up the same questions of justice and power in philosophy.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Thucydides said eyewitnesses remember the same event differently. Why do you think that happens?
  2. Pericles said Athens was a "school" for the rest of Greece. What would you want your town or country to teach others?
  3. The Athenians told the Melians that the strong do what they can. Do you agree? What could the Melians have said back?
  4. Thucydides wanted his book to be useful forever. What lesson from history do you think everyone should know?
  5. He was exiled for failing at his job, and then he became one of the greatest historians. What good can come out of a failure?

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Socrates lived in Athens about 2,400 years ago. He did not write books. He walked around the city asking people questions: What is courage? What is fairness? What makes a person good? Most people thought they knew the answers, until Socrates asked a few more questions.

A friend once asked the priestess of the god Apollo at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer came back: no one. Socrates was puzzled, because he did not think he was wise. So he went to people who were famous for being wise and questioned them. He found that they did not really know what they claimed to know. He decided that his only wisdom was this: he knew that he did not know.

Some powerful people grew tired of his questions. When Socrates was about 70, three men took him to court. A jury of about 500 citizens found him guilty, and he was sentenced to death. His friends offered to help him escape from prison, but he said no: he had lived under the laws of Athens all his life, and he would not break them now.
His student Plato wrote down the story in four short books: Euthyphro, the Apology (which means a speech of defense, not saying sorry), Crito and Phaedo.

blocks.name: gb-last-days
blocks.cap: Step through Socrates' last days. On the trial, switch votes and see how close the verdict was.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Play Socrates. Pick a word everyone uses, like fair or brave. Ask someone in your family what it means. Then think of an example that doesn't fit their answer (“Is it brave to run into traffic for a ball?”). Help them improve the answer. Take turns. You are doing what Socrates did: testing an idea with questions.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Socrates (c. 470–399 BC) spent his life in Athens, served as a soldier in the Peloponnesian War, and became famous for questioning people in public. He wrote nothing. We know him through his students, above all Plato (c. 428–348 BC), through the soldier and writer Xenophon, and through a comedy, Aristophanes' Clouds (423 BC), which made fun of him.

In 399 BC, a few years after Athens lost the war with Sparta, three citizens, Meletus, Anytus and Lycon, charged Socrates with impiety (not honoring the city's gods and bringing in new ones) and with corrupting the young. Many historians think politics played a part: some of Socrates' companions had been tied to the harsh rulers who governed Athens just after the war. The charges themselves were religious ones.
Plato tells the story in four dialogues. They are short, and they are the best place to start reading Plato.

On his way to court, Socrates meets Euthyphro, an expert in religious matters who is taking his own father to court over a worker's death, and is sure that this is the holy thing to do. Socrates asks him what holiness is. Euthyphro gives an example, then a definition (“what the gods love”), then a better one (“what all the gods love”). Socrates then asks the famous question:

This is the Euthyphro question. If the gods love something because it is holy, then holiness is something in its own right, and “loved by the gods” only describes it. If something is holy only because the gods love it, holiness seems to depend on their choice. Euthyphro picks the first, which means his definition did not say what holiness is. Philosophers and religious thinkers have discussed the question ever since, and have given many different answers.
“Apology” comes from the Greek apologia, a speech of defense. Socrates tells the jury he is no clever speaker, then explains how his habit of questioning began, with the oracle at Delphi.

He cross-examines his accuser Meletus in front of the jury, catching him in contradictions. He says he is like a gadfly sent to keep a large, sleepy horse awake: the city needs someone to sting it into thinking. He says he has always followed an inner voice, his daimonion, which warns him when he is about to do something wrong.

The jury votes him guilty. By the usual reckoning the vote was about 280 to 220, and Socrates remarks that thirty votes the other way would have freed him. In Athens the accused then proposed a penalty. Socrates first says that he deserves free meals at public expense, like an Olympic champion, and then offers a fine his friends will pay. The jury votes for death. Here is part of his reason for not simply going quietly into exile:

blocks.name: gb-last-days
blocks.cap: Move the slider on the trial scene to see how many votes had to change. In Athens a tie set the accused free.

blocks.title: Thirty votes
blocks.q: Suppose a jury of 500 voted 280 guilty and 220 not guilty, and a tie means acquittal. How many jurors would have had to change their vote?
steps: Each switched vote takes one from 280 and adds one to 220, so the gap of 60 closes by 2 each time.
After 30 switches the vote is 250 to 250, a tie.
A tie acquits, so 30 votes would have been enough.

blocks.html: Socrates waits about a month in prison, because no executions could happen until a sacred ship returned from the island of Delos. His old friend Crito comes before dawn: the guards are paid, and friends will hide him in Thessaly. Socrates says they must reason it out, as always. They agree on a starting point:

Socrates then imagines the Laws of Athens speaking to him. They raised and educated him; for seventy years he was free to leave and chose to stay; that is a kind of agreement. If he runs now, he does wrong in return for wrong, which he holds is never right. He stays.

The argument in the Crito is one of the first statements of the idea that living in a society can be a kind of agreement with its laws. Later writers, from Locke to Rousseau on this ladder, built theories of a social contract. Others have read the same dialogue as a case for following one's conscience, because in the Apology Socrates also says he would not stop questioning even if the court ordered him to. Readers still argue about how the two fit together.
Thinking “apology” means Socrates said sorry. He did the opposite: he defended his whole way of life and refused to beg.
The last day, spent talking about whether the soul outlives the body, is the next rung on this ladder. It ends with Socrates drinking the poison, calmly, among his friends.

Plato or Socrates? Plato was in the courtroom (he says so in the Apology) but these are his works, written years later. Scholars think the Apology is fairly close to what Socrates said, but nobody can be sure how much is Plato's own.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Three sources disagree. Aristophanes' Clouds shows a fussy teacher who studies the sky and teaches tricks of argument for money, which Socrates denies in the Apology. Xenophon's Memorabilia and his own short Apology show a practical, pious man giving sound advice. Plato's Socrates is ironic, probing and always asking “what is it?” Historians call the puzzle of the real Socrates the Socratic problem.

Socrates' way of questioning has a Greek name, elenchus, “testing” or “refutation”. Someone offers a definition; Socrates gets agreement on some other points; then he shows that those points contradict the definition. The person ends up puzzled. Socrates thought puzzlement was progress, because you cannot look for an answer you think you already have. Teachers and lawyers still use a version of this method.

items: Is it ever right to break a law? What would Socrates in the Crito say, and what would Socrates in the Apology say?
Does knowing that you don't know make you wiser than someone who is sure?
If a jury is fair but makes a wrong decision, should you still accept it?

blocks.html: Later books answer back. Aristotle (on this ladder) named the Socratic “what is it?” question as the start of the search for definitions. The Stoics, such as Epictetus, made Socrates their model of calm in the face of death. Martin Luther King Jr.'s “Letter from Birmingham Jail” (1963) points to Socrates when it explains breaking an unjust law openly and accepting the penalty.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Socrates said he was wise only because he knew he didn't know. Can you think of a time when admitting you didn't know something helped you?
  2. Was Socrates right to stay in prison when his friends could have helped him escape? What would you have told him?
  3. Socrates said “the unexamined life is not worth living.” What do you think it means to examine your life?
  4. Is something good because people like it, or do people like it because it is good? Try it with a game, a food and an act of kindness.
  5. Socrates called himself a gadfly that keeps a city awake. Is it helpful or annoying to have someone around who questions everything? Both?
  6. Why do you think Plato wrote these books as conversations instead of essays?

blocks.html: A note for parents: This dialogue is about death, and it ends with Socrates drinking poison, as his sentence required. Plato tells it gently, without anything graphic. It presents Socrates' own beliefs about the soul; families will want to talk about their own.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

The Phaedo tells the story of Socrates' last day. His friends came to the prison early in the morning, because they knew it was the day the sentence would be carried out. Some of them were crying. Socrates was calm, and even cheerful.

He spent the day doing what he loved most: talking and asking questions. The big question was this: does the soul go on living after the body dies? Socrates believed it does, and he tried to give reasons, not just say so. His friends Simmias and Cebes raised objections, and he welcomed them.

One of his arguments used opposites. Sleeping turns into waking, and waking into sleeping. Small things grow large, and large things can shrink. Things come from their opposites. So, Socrates asked, if living things die, might the dead also come back to life?

blocks.name: gb-opposites
blocks.cap: Pick a pair of opposites. Each one turns into the other by its own road.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Opposites hunt. List as many pairs of opposites as you can in five minutes (hot and cold, full and empty, wet and dry…). For each pair, name the change that goes each way: what turns hot into cold? What turns cold into hot? Are there any pairs where the change only goes one way?
Socrates said that swans sing most beautifully just before they die, not out of sadness but out of joy. People still call someone's last great work a “swan song.”

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Plato's Phaedo (written about 380s BC) is told by Phaedo, one of the young men who were there, to a friend named Echecrates some time afterward. Phaedo lists who came. Plato himself was absent: “Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill,” Phaedo says (in Jowett’s translation), a small and moving touch from the author.

Socrates' wife Xanthippe is there at dawn with their youngest child, and Socrates has her taken home. He tells his friends that he has been setting Aesop's fables to verse, because a dream kept telling him to “make music.” Then the conversation turns serious.

Why is Socrates not afraid? He says a lover of wisdom spends his life trying to see things with the mind, not the body's senses, and death, as he believes, is the soul's release from the body. So a philosopher has been rehearsing all along:

head: Argument
In brief
The objection it faces
rows: Everything that has an opposite comes from that opposite, so the living come from the dead, as the dead from the living.
It shows at most that souls return; Cebes wants to know that they last.
We recognize two sticks as “equal” but not perfectly equal, so we must already know Equality itself. We learned it before birth.
This shows the soul existed before birth, not that it survives death.
The soul is like the unseen, unchanging and divine; the body is like the seen and changing. So the soul is not the kind of thing that scatters.
Simmias: maybe the soul is like the tuning of a lyre, which vanishes when the lyre breaks.
The soul brings life to whatever it is in, as fire brings heat. So it cannot admit death, as fire cannot admit cold.
Socrates himself says the starting points need further study.
blocks.cap: The arguments of the Phaedo, in our own words.

blocks.name: gb-opposites
blocks.cap: The first argument: each pair of opposites is joined by two roads. Socrates asks what would happen if the change ran only one way.

blocks.html: Simmias and Cebes go quiet, worried that their doubts will upset him on such a day. Socrates laughs and says he is no more troubled than a swan:

Simmias says the soul might be a kind of harmony, like the tuning of a lyre. Cebes says it might be like a weaver who wears out many cloaks and then dies: it outlasts many bodies but not for ever. At this low point Socrates warns against becoming a “hater of arguments” (a misologist) just because some arguments fail. The fault, he says, is in our skill, not in reasoning itself.

Before his last argument, Socrates tells how, as a young man, he hoped the philosopher Anaxagoras would explain why things are as they are, by showing what is best. He was disappointed: Anaxagoras explained only the bones and muscles, so to speak, not the reasons. So Socrates turned to a “second voyage”: looking for causes in the Forms, such as Beauty itself and Largeness itself.

Thinking the Phaedo proves the soul is immortal. Socrates offers arguments and says they deserve more testing; he ends with a story about the next world and says only that a sensible man would not insist it is exactly true, but that it is worth the risk of believing something like it.

At sunset Socrates bathes, says goodbye to his family, and drinks the cup when the jailer brings it, as the law requires. He asks Crito to offer a rooster to Asclepius, the god of healing; readers still debate what he meant. Phaedo ends:

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Phaedo is one of the first dialogues to rely on what are now called Plato's Forms: Equality itself, Beauty itself, Justice itself, perfect and unchanging, which particular things only resemble. The recollection argument here links back to the Meno, where a boy “recollects” geometry. The Republic, later on this ladder, builds the Forms into a whole picture of knowledge.

Aristotle, in On the Soul, describes the soul as the form of a living body, which made the question of its surviving the body much harder. Plotinus and Augustine, later on this ladder, drew on the Phaedo, each in his own way. Some modern readers find the arguments weak but the portrait of Socrates' calm unforgettable; others think the arguments are better than they first look. The harmony objection anticipates the modern view that the mind depends on the brain, and the dialogue is still read in courses on that question.

items: Is it possible to face death without fear? What helped Socrates?
If an argument for something you hope is true turns out weak, should you stop believing it, keep looking for better arguments, or both?
Socrates warned against “hating arguments.” Have you ever given up on reasoning because one argument let you down?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Socrates' friends were sad, but he was calm. Why do you think he felt that way?
  2. What other opposites can you think of? Do they really turn into each other?
  3. Simmias compared the soul to the music of a lyre. Is that a good comparison? Why or why not?
  4. What is a “swan song”? Can you think of an example?
  5. Phaedo calls Socrates “the wisest and justest and best.” What would you like people to say about you?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
A young man named Meno asks Socrates a question: Can goodness be taught? Socrates says he can't answer that, because he doesn't even know what goodness is. Can Meno tell him?

Meno tries, but every answer has a problem. He gets frustrated and says talking to Socrates is like touching an electric fish: it leaves you numb! Then he asks a tricky question: how can you search for something if you don't know what it is? Even if you found it, how would you know?

Socrates answers with an experiment. He calls over a boy who has never studied geometry. He draws a square in the sand and asks: how can we make a square exactly twice as big? The boy guesses wrong twice. But Socrates never tells him the answer. He only asks questions, and in the end the boy sees it for himself: build the new square on the line from corner to corner, the diagonal.

blocks.name: gb-meno-square
blocks.cap: Follow the boy's guesses and then the answer, one step at a time.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Double a square with paper. Cut out a paper square. Fold it corner to corner both ways, so the creases make an X. Now fold each corner in to the center. You have a new square with half the area. Unfold it: the original square is double the folded one, and the folded square's side runs along the diagonal of a quarter of the big one. Can you explain why to someone else, using only questions?

Socrates thought this showed that the boy already had the knowledge somewhere inside him, and the questions helped him remember it. Not everyone agrees with that idea. But everyone agrees the boy learned something real.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

The Meno (about 385 BC) is short and lively. Meno is a wealthy young man from Thessaly, in northern Greece, visiting Athens; he has studied with the famous speaker Gorgias. He opens with no warm-up at all:
“Virtue” here translates the Greek aretē: excellence, being good at being a person. Socrates says he can't say how virtue is acquired until he knows what it is.

items: A list: a man's virtue is managing the city's affairs, a woman's is managing a household, and so on. Socrates says he asked for one thing and got a swarm, like asking what a bee is and being shown many bees.
The power to rule. But is that a virtue in a child, or in someone who rules unjustly?
Wanting good things and being able to get them, justly. But justice is part of virtue, so the definition uses what it is trying to define.

blocks.html: Meno, stuck, complains:
The torpedo fish is the electric ray. Socrates replies that he numbs others only because he is numb himself: he is puzzled too.

Meno's paradox: you cannot search for what you know (you already have it) or for what you do not know (you would not know what to look for, or recognize it if you found it). So inquiry seems impossible.

Socrates answers with a teaching he says he heard from priests and poets: the soul is immortal and has learned everything before; so what we call learning is really recollection. He offers to show it.

Socrates calls over one of Meno's servants, a boy who speaks Greek but has never studied geometry (he was a slave, as many household servants in Athens were). Socrates draws a square with sides of two feet and asks for the side of a square twice the size.

blocks.name: gb-meno-square
blocks.cap: The lesson as Plato tells it: two wrong guesses, then the diagonal.

blocks.title: Why the diagonal works
blocks.q: A square has side 2, so area 4. Show that the square built on its diagonal has area 8.
steps: Put four copies of the square together to make a big square of side 4 and area 16.
Draw the diagonal of each small square so the four diagonals form a tilted square inside.
Each diagonal cuts its small square in half, and the tilted square is made of four halves: $4 \times 2 = 8$.
So the square on the diagonal is twice the original. (In modern terms, the diagonal is $2\sqrt2 \approx 2.83$, and $(2\sqrt2)^2 = 8$.)

blocks.html: When the boy's guesses fail, Socrates points out that he is now better off: before he thought he knew, now he knows that he doesn't, and he will want to find out. At the end, Socrates draws the lesson:

Thinking the boy just guessed until he got lucky. Every step is a question the boy answers by looking at the drawing. Whether that is “recollection” is a philosophical claim; that the boy reasoned his way there is plain in the text.

Socrates now reasons from a hypothesis, as geometers do: if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it can be taught. But then there should be teachers of it. Anytus, an Athenian politician who will later be one of Socrates' accusers, joins in and angrily rejects the paid teachers called sophists. Socrates points out that even famous good Athenians, like Pericles, did not manage to make their sons good.

So Socrates suggests that good leaders may act on true opinion rather than knowledge. True opinion guides you as well as knowledge does, as long as it lasts, but it is like the moving statues of the legendary sculptor Daedalus: it runs away unless it is tied down. Working out the reason why ties it down and turns it into knowledge.

Knowledge vs. true opinion: a person who has been to Larissa and someone who has only guessed the right road will both get you there. The difference is that knowledge is tied down by a reason and stays put. Philosophers still discuss this distinction.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Meno links the early dialogues, where Socrates questions and nobody reaches an answer, with Plato's bigger theories. Recollection returns in the Phaedo as an argument for the soul. The geometry example points to the Republic, where mathematics trains the mind to see beyond the senses. And the question “what is knowledge, and how does it differ from true opinion?” is the subject of the Theaetetus.

Aristotle mentions the Meno's puzzle in his Posterior Analytics and gives his own answer: we know some things in a general way and others in particular, so we can learn from what we partly know. Much later, the question of whether some knowledge is inborn divided the rationalists (Descartes, Leibniz) from the empiricists (Locke, Hume). Teachers today speak of “Socratic questioning” when they lead students to find answers themselves, as in this lesson.

items: Did the boy learn geometry, or remember it, or work it out? What would count as evidence?
Can goodness be taught? If so, by whom: parents, teachers, books, friends?
Why might knowing why something is true make it stick better than just knowing that it is true?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Can goodness be taught? Think of someone who taught you to be kind or honest. How did they do it?
  2. Is it better to be told an answer, or to work it out with help? When is each one better?
  3. The boy felt stuck before he found the answer. Have you ever felt stuck right before you learned something?
  4. What is the difference between guessing the right answer and knowing it?
  5. Meno said Socrates was like an electric fish. Is it a good thing to be puzzled? Why?
